The verse describes a demand, or supplication, by which someone calls for the punishment of the disbelievers. God declares that this punishment is certain and that no one can repel it, since it comes from God, the Lord of the ascents and degrees. The commentators report that the one who made the demand was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said: "O God, if this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us from the sky." Some read it as a mocking challenge. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others connect the verse to this cry, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi discuss the grammar of the preposition bi and the sense of the verb sa'ala, close to "ask for" or "demand insistently". As for the reading without the hamza, Ibn Jinni, Abu Hayyan and al-Razi take it either as a lightened form or as a derivative of "flowing", naming a valley of Hell called Sa'il, according to Zayd ibn Thabit.

The following part, which describes a day lasting fifty thousand years, divides the scholars. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid takes it to be the distance between the bottom of the seventh earth and the Throne, while Ibn Ishaq takes it as the time that human beings would need for the climb. Ikrima, and others reported by Ibn Kathir, take it as the lifespan of the world. Ibn Abbas, according to Ibn Kathir, declined to rule on the matter when questioned. Hadiths cited by al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir say that the day will be light for the believer.

On the meaning of "al-ruh", opinions differ: Gabriel for Ibn Abbas and most, another creature for Abu Salih, or the soul of the deceased for Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb. Finally, all agree that the Prophet is commanded to bear with patience, which Ibn Juzayy and al-Tabari link to steadfastness against mockery, while Ibn Zayd sees an instruction later abrogated by the command to fight.

This verse states that a punishment demanded by a questioner will certainly befall the disbelievers, and that no one can repel it, since it comes from God, Lord of the ascending degrees and of bounties. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi report, with Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, that the questioner was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who asked God to rain stones from heaven upon them. Others, such as Ibn Juzayy and al-Zamakhshari, explain that the verb may mean to inquire or to press for haste, and may refer to Abu Jahl or a group of Quraysh. The word al-ma'arij is taken by Ibn Abbas to mean the heavens, by Qatada to mean God's favours, and by Mujahid to mean the stairways of the heavens. Regarding the day whose measure is fifty thousand years, most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ikrima, identify it as the Day of Judgement, while Mujahid understands it as the distance between the lowest earth and the Throne, and Ikrima as the lifespan of the world. Al-Tabari cites a hadith in which that day is lightened for the believer. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the figure may also express the severity of a hard day. As for the unhamzated reading sala, scholars differ between a softened form of sa'ala and a derivation from flowing, which would refer to a valley in Hell called Sa'il, according to Zayd ibn Thabit.

The commentators explain that this verse reports the request of those who mockingly demanded the punishment. Mujahid understands it as the disbelievers calling down a punishment on themselves that will fall in the hereafter, and Ibn Abbas and as-Suddi relate that the one who asked was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said: If this is truly from You, rain down on us stones from the sky. The meaning is that this punishment will surely fall upon the disbelievers, for none can repel it, since God has decreed it. He is called Dhu al-Ma'arij, the Lord of ascents, that is of elevation, grace and bounty. For Ibn Abbas the ma'arij are the heavens through which the angels ascend, for Qatada they are the favours and bounties, and for al-Hasan the rungs leading to heaven. Most take the Spirit to be Gabriel. Qatada, Ikrima, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd connect the day of fifty thousand years to the Day of Resurrection, while Mujahid holds that it is the distance from the lowest earth to the Throne which the angels would cover. Others understand it as the lifespan of this world. All agree that the patience commanded is a patience free of complaint, but they differ on its occasion: al-Hasan links it to the accusations of madness, sorcery and poetry, while Ibn Zayd links it to the disbelief before the command to fight. The commentators do not settle the exact length of that day or the precise nature of the terrors accompanying it.

This verse says that the angels and the Spirit ascend to God on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years. Most commentators identify the Spirit with Gabriel, and take "to Him" to mean God, with the ascent understood as rising to the place from which His commands descend. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan, Ikrima and al-Dahhak say this day is the Day of Resurrection, which will last fifty thousand years for the disbelievers. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in which the day is lightened for the believer until it is no longer than an obligatory prayer, while noting that some of its transmitters are weak.

Other readings are also given. Mujahid, as reported by al-Tabari, takes the distance to be from the bottom of the seventh earth to the Throne, and Wahb ibn Munabbih measures it from the surface of the earth to the Throne. Some hold that the figure stands for the whole duration of the world, a view attributed to Mujahid and Ikrima, who say no one knows how much has passed or how much remains. Al-Hasan understands it as the length of the reckoning, and al-Kalbi says that if created beings had conducted the reckoning it would last fifty thousand years, whereas God completes it in an instant.

Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir link this verse to the verse in Surat al-Sajda that mentions a day of a thousand years, explaining that the distance from the lowest heaven to the earth is a thousand years, while the distance from the depths of the world to the Throne is fifty thousand. In either case the commentators stress that the length may express the severity of that day rather than an exact count.

Finally, God commands His Prophet to bear patiently with the rejection of his people, and some commentators note that this command was later abrogated by the order to fight.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to be patient with the harm and denial of his people, with a beautiful patience, meaning a patience free of complaint or distress voiced to anyone other than God, as al-Tabari, al-Samani and al-Qurtubi explain. Most commentators connect this command to the preceding verses, which describe the unbelievers asking mockingly and defiantly for the punishment to come. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid identify the questioner as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy treat the context more broadly. They agree that the patience meant is one free from despair and impatience. Al-Hasan understands it as outward courtesy, whereas Ibn Zayd holds that it was abrogated by the verses on fighting, a view al-Tabari rejects as unsupported, arguing that the Prophet was always commanded to be patient. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the command came before permission to fight was given. The overall message is consolation and steadfastness: the Prophet should not be distressed by their rejection, because the punishment will surely befall them, even though they consider it far off.

In this verse God says that the disbelievers consider the promised punishment far off, because they deny resurrection, reckoning and recompense, whereas God sees it as near, since whatever is coming is near. The commentators generally take the pronoun "they see it" to refer to the punishment. Al-Razi offers a second reading in which it refers to the day whose length is fifty thousand years, meaning that the disbelievers regard it as impossible. Al-Mawardi and others explain "far" either as impossible and never to happen, or as something the disbelievers deem unlikely. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baqa'i take the distance to mean that they regard it as unattainable. Al-Tabari explains that nearness concerns possibility rather than time, while Ibn 'Ashur and al-Jaza'iri read it as a statement that the punishment will certainly occur. Several exegetes report that the verse answers mocking challengers who demanded the punishment, and that the Prophet was ordered to be patient, some adding that this preceded the command to fight. The commentators agree that the verse exposes the disbelievers' delusion through the security and comfort they enjoy, and that God knows His promise will certainly be fulfilled. As for the day intended, opinions differ between the Day of Judgment, the duration of the worldly life and another view, and none is preferred over the others here.

The commentators explain that this verse comes in the context of the disbelievers' denial and their demand for the punishment to be hastened. God says that they regard that punishment as far off, because they deny the resurrection and recompense, while He sees it as near, since whatever is coming is near. Most agree on this sense: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari take distance to mean that the event is far from happening and nearness to mean that it is imminent. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi understand the distant as what seems impossible to reason and the near as what is easy for divine power. Ibn 'Ashur sees a figure of speech for implausibility and for the certainty of fulfilment, and a reason for the command to be patient. Ibn Juzayy notes that the pronoun may refer to the punishment or to the Day, and that nearness may be temporal or relative to God's power. Some, such as al-A'mash, hold that it refers to resurrection, which they reject as impossible. All see the verse as a consolation to the Prophet and a call to patience before his people. Ibn Zayd holds that the command to patience was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others consider it still in force.

This verse describes the terror of the Day of Resurrection, when the sky will be like molten metal, like the dregs of oil or melted ore, and the mountains will be like carded, dyed wool scattered by the wind. Ibn Abbas explained al-muhl as the sediment of oil, Ibn Mas'ud as molten lead, copper and silver, Mujahid as pus mixed with blood, and al-Hasan as melted silver. The commentators agree on the image of melting and changing colour, but differ on the substance. As for al-ihn, most take it as dyed wool, al-Hasan as red wool, the weakest kind, and Muqatil as carded wool, pointing to lightness, scattering and varied colours. On the phrase 'no close friend will ask after his friend', most explain that each person is absorbed in his own plight, while Ibn Zayd and others understand that no one will be asked for anything. On 'they will see them', Ibn Abbas and Qatada say that relatives recognise one another and then flee, Mujahid that believers see the disbelievers, and Ibn Zayd that followers see those who misled them in the Fire; al-Tabari prefers the first reading as the one best suited to the context. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the pronoun may refer to the punishment or to the day, and that the nearness mentioned may be nearness in time or in possibility.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the sky becomes like al-muhl, meaning the dregs of oil or molten metal as Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud explain, and the mountains become like wool (al-'ihn). The commentators agree that the verse conveys the extreme terror of that day, when the order of the cosmos dissolves and the mountains, once so firm, soften and scatter. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take 'ihn to mean wool, while al-Hasan limits it to red wool; al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also note that it refers to wool dyed in various colours, matching the varied hues of the mountains. Al-Qurtubi reports from al-Hasan that the mountains pass through stages: shifting sand, then carded wool, then scattered dust. On the phrase that no close friend will ask another, the commentators agree that each person is absorbed in his own plight, as Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di explain. The meaning of 'they will be shown to one another' is disputed: Ibn Abbas and Qatada hold that relatives recognise one another and then flee; Mujahid says the believers see the disbelievers; Ibn Zayd says the misled see those who misled them in the Fire. Al-Tabari prefers the first view as fitting the context of the verses, and Ibn Kathir also mentions it.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when a close relative will not ask another close relative about his condition, because each is preoccupied with himself. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain it this way, and Ibn Kathir cites Qatada. The commentators agree that hamim means a close relative or intimate friend, and that the lack of questioning comes from terror and preoccupation with oneself, as other verses confirm: each of them that day will have a concern that suffices him. They differ on the meaning of yubassarunahum (they will see one another). Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abbas, say that relatives recognize one another and then flee from each other. Mujahid holds that the believers see the disbelievers, while Ibn Zayd holds that the disbelievers see those who misled them into the Fire. As for the recitation, most readers have yas'alu with a fatha, while Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read yus'alu with a damma, meaning that no one will be asked about his intimate. Al-Tabari prefers the fatha because the readers agree upon it. The following verses say that the guilty one would wish to ransom himself with his children, spouse, brother, clan and everyone on earth, but that this would not save him, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi state. The commentators read this passage as a way of expressing the extreme severity of that day.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment: the criminal, meaning the disbeliever according to most commentators, would wish to ransom himself from that day's punishment with his dearest ones, his sons, his wife, his brother, and the clan that sheltered him, and even with everyone on earth, so that it might save him. The commentators explain that the horror of that day is so great that no one asks after a close relative, each being absorbed in himself, although they can see one another. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the fasila is the nearest kin, while Abu 'Ubayda places it below the tribe, Tha'lab takes it to mean the nearest forefathers, and Malik takes it to mean the mother who raised him. Al-Mawardi and others understand it as the clan that supports him.

The word "kalla" rejects this wish: no ransom will be accepted and no kinship will save him. The commentators explain that "Laza" is a name of Hell, at times the second of its levels, which tears away the limbs. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take shawa to mean the scalp, Abu Salih the limbs, al-Hasan the beauty of the face, and al-Dahhak the flesh down to the bone. It calls those who turned their backs on the truth and gathered wealth without giving it away. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir treat the calling as literal, whereas al-Khalil and Tha'lab read it as a figure of speech for destruction or drawing close.

This passage from Surah al-Ma'arij describes the Day of Judgement, when the criminal would wish to ransom himself from punishment with those he loves most. The commentators explain that he would offer his sons, his wife, his brother, and his closest kin who sheltered him, even everyone on earth, and then be saved. Al-Tabari notes that the order runs from the most beloved to the nearest, with the sons first because ransoming with them shows the depth of the distress. All agree that the companion is the wife and that the brother is the known brother, but they differ on fasila. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it as the tribe or clan, Abu 'Ubayda as something smaller than a tribe, Tha'lab as the nearest ancestors, while Ashhab reports from Malik that it means the mother, and al-Mubarrad compares it to a limb cut off from the body. As for tu'wihi, some read it as protection through kinship, others as support in calamities. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya see the wish as unrealisable, with thumma indicating how unlikely this rescue is. God's rebuttal, kalla, rejects the wish. The exegetes then differ on shawa: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as the scalp, al-Hasan as the features of the face, Abu Salih as the extremities of the limbs, and Ibn Jubayr as the sinews. Finally, the Fire calls those who turned away, refused, and hoarded wealth without spending it; some take this literally and others as an image of perdition.

This verse describes the terror of the Day of Judgment, when the guilty one would wish to ransom himself from punishment with those dearest to him: his sons, his wife, his brother, and his close kin who sheltered him, and even everyone on earth, if that could save him. The commentators explain fasila as the nearest kin or clan, with al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Mawardi noting that Mujahid called it the tribe, and Abu 'Ubayda holding that it is smaller than the qabila. Tha'lab took it to mean the closest ancestors, while Malik, as reported by al-Qurtubi and al-Mawardi, said it refers to his mother who raised him. Most agree that the guilty one is the unbeliever, and that such a ransom would not save him, which is why the verse answers with a firm 'no'. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report differing views on the shawa that the Fire strips away: the scalp according to Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, the limbs and extremities according to Abu Salih and Qatada, and the flesh away from the bone according to al-Dahhak. The Fire then calls those who turned their backs and gathered wealth without paying its due, a warning that the commentators draw from this verse.

These verses describe the wish of the guilty, meaning the disbeliever, on the Day of Judgment: he would like to ransom himself from punishment by offering his sons, his wife, his brother, his clan that sheltered him, and even everyone on earth, and then be saved by that ransom. The commentators agree that this wish will not be granted, and God rejects it with the word "No", so no ransom will save him. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain the word fasilatihi as his clan or tribe, al-Tha'labi reports that others take it to mean his closest forefathers, Abu 'Ubayda says it is smaller than a tribe, and Ashhab reports from Malik that it means his mother. All agree that the wife is his spouse. For "and whoever is on earth, all of them", al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud read the word then as signalling improbability, meaning that salvation remains unlikely even with such a ransom. On tu'wihi, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd take it as support, while al-Dahhak takes it as being gathered into one's lineage. Most scholars take Laza as a name of Hell, while al-Dahhak places it at the eighth level. On "nazza'atan lil-shawa", most say it tears away the limbs, but they differ on the meaning of shawa: Mujahid says the scalp, Ibn Jubayr the sinews and heels, al-Hasan the face's beauty, and Abu Salih the extremities of the hands and feet. On "tad'u man adbara wa tawalla", al-Farra' understands that it calls them by name, al-Khalil sees it as an image of its greed, and Tha'lab reads it as destruction. Finally, "jama'a fa-awda" is read by the commentators as hoarding wealth and withholding God's due from it.

This verse, in the Surah of the Ascending Stairways, answers the disbelieving person who, on the Day of Judgement, wishes to ransom himself from punishment with his sons, his wife, his brother, his kin and everyone on earth. God says "kallā", meaning no: no ransom will save him. He then explains that Laẓā is a name of Hell, named for its blazing intensity. The commentators agree on the general sense that ransom is useless and that the fire is what the pronoun "innahā" refers to. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir report that this fire strips away the skin, and opinions differ on the meaning of "al-shawā". Mujahid and Ibn Abbas take it to mean the scalp, citing al-A'sha's verse; Abu Salih takes it to mean the hands and feet; Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the sinews and heels; al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliya, the beauty of the face; al-Dahhak, the flesh and skin pulled from the bone. Al-Tabari favours the sense of limbs and scalp, and notes that the widely transmitted reading is the nominative, while the accusative is also grammatically valid. Several exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, link to this fire the fact that it calls those who turned away, who amassed wealth and withheld God's due. Ibn Abbas and al-Zamakhshari take the calling as literal, al-Khalil and al-Razi as a figure of speech. The overall reading is a condemnation of the one who hoarded wealth and refused to give what was owed from it.

This verse describes the Fire called Laza, which strips away the extremities and the scalp, as al-Tabari and his chains of transmission report. The commentators agree on the general sense: the flame devours whatever is not a vital spot, and the body is then renewed for further punishment. On the reading, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi note that most readers use the nominative nazzaʿatun, while Hafs reads the accusative nazzaʿatan; al-Tabari prefers the nominative because the readers of the great cities agree on it. The meaning of al-shawa is disputed. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿAta', Saʿid ibn Jubayr and others take it as the skin of the head or skin and skull; Abu Salih takes it as the extremities of the hands and feet or the calf flesh; al-Hasan and Abu al-ʿAliya understand the beauty of the face; al-Dahhak takes it as flesh and skin stripped from the bone; Ibn Jubayr as the sinews and heels; and al-Tabari gives the general sense of whatever is not fatal. As to the calling of the Fire, Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Kathir take it literally, calling by name those who turned away from the truth, while al-Khalil reads it as a figure for the Fire's grip on them, and Tha'lab reads it as destruction; al-Zamakhshari also mentions the guardians of Hell. The commentators explain that those called are those who turned their backs, rejected faith, and hoarded wealth without giving God's due. Finally, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the guilty person would wish to ransom himself with his children, his family and everyone on earth, but this will not be accepted.

This verse says that Hell, called Laza, calls out to and draws in those who turned away from the truth, turned their backs on obedience, and hoarded wealth without paying God's due from it. The commentators differ on the nature of this calling. Ibn Abbas and others take it literally: the Fire addresses the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names and their fathers' names in an eloquent voice, then gathers them up as a bird pecks up grain. Some add that God gives it the power of speech, as He gives speech to the skins and hands. Al-Khalil and Tha'lab understand the word as meaning destruction or summoning, so that Hell brings them in. Al-Farra' sees it as calling each person by name, like saying 'O disbeliever, come to me'. Others treat the calling as a metaphor, or attribute it to the guardians of Hell. On turning away and turning back, all agree it means rejecting faith and obedience. On hoarding, the verse refers to storing wealth without paying zakat or other dues; Qatada describes this man as one who gathered and withheld. The setting is a Day when no one can ransom another, not by children, spouse, brother, clan, or everything on earth. As to the Fire stripping the scalp and the extremities, the commentators offer several readings of shawa: the skin of the head, the flesh beneath the skin, the limbs, or the face's noble features.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of the people of the Fire: Hell calls out to those who turned their backs on the truth and withdrew from it, and then it is said of them that they gathered wealth and hoarded it in a container, withholding God's right from it. The apparent meaning, on which most agree, is accumulation and miserliness. Mujahid says it means gathering wealth, and Qatada adds that he was one who gathered and withheld for the wicked. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir read in the phrase an allusion to greed and long hope, and a rebuke of one who hoards without paying zakat and his due obligations, and who is so occupied with his property that he neglects religion. Ibn 'Ashur links these traits to the mindset of polytheism that turns its adherents away from the call to Islam.

On the verb "calls" (tad'u), opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nasafi and al-Baghawi hold that Hell calls the disbelievers and hypocrites by their names in a clear tongue and then seizes them like a bird pecking grain; al-Razi and Ibn Kathir also take this literally. Al-Khalil, Tha'lab and al-Zamakhshari understand it as meaning to destroy or to draw near, and Ibn 'Atiyya sees it as an image of the pull exerted upon them. Ibn Juzayy reports that the call refers to Hell taking them in charge.

As for the word shawa, most exegetes take it to mean the scalp, while Abu Salih understands the extremities of the hands and feet, and some take it as the limbs in general apart from vital parts. On this point the commentators agree that the fire tears away the skin and the limbs.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the human being as created anxious and greedy, one who panics when harm touches him and becomes stingy when good comes to him. They largely agree that the word halu' means intense greed combined with great distress and weak patience, and that the verse is explained by what follows it: harm makes him wail, good makes him withhold. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Ikrima, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Mujahid give closely related meanings such as greedy, impatient, miserly and complaining. Al-Tabari and several others take the term here to refer to the disbeliever, while others hold that it applies to humankind in general, the exception that follows including those who pray. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi regard this trait as a disposition created in a person which can nonetheless be struggled against. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes anxiety, a weakness of the soul, from tenderness of heart, which is a virtue. As for the exception, most commentators mention those who are constant in their prayer, meaning those who guard it at its times, and some add paying zakat, belief in the Last Day, and guarding chastity and trusts. They differ on the meaning of constancy: Ibn Mas'ud takes it as keeping to the prescribed times, 'Uqba ibn 'Amir as not turning the head during prayer, and Ibn Jurayj as performing many voluntary prayers. Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari cite a hadith that the deed most beloved to God is the most constant, even if small.

God describes man as created anxious and greedy. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, explain al-hal' as extreme impatience joined with intense covetousness: a person panics when harm such as poverty or sickness strikes, and grows stingy when good fortune comes. Ibn Abbas held that the following words explain the term, and most exegetes agreed. Ikrima and Qatada described the person as impatient, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak as miserly, Sa'id ibn Jubayr as tight-fisted, and Mujahid as greedy. Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi took the word 'man' to mean the disbeliever, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy took it to mean humankind in general, which allows the exception that follows. Ibn al-Qayyim links anxiety to weak faith in divine decree, and notes that tenderness of heart is a different thing. The verse then excepts those who pray constantly. Ibn Mas'ud took constancy to mean keeping the prescribed times, Ibn Jurayj meant frequent voluntary prayer, and 'Uqba ibn 'Amir meant not turning one's gaze during prayer. Many commentators add further traits to the exception, such as giving the due share of wealth, guarding chastity, keeping trusts and covenants, and bearing true witness.

This verse describes the person who loses self-control: when hardship strikes he grows distressed and despairing, and when good fortune comes he becomes stingy and withholding. Commentators explain the word halu' (anxious greed) in several ways, as excessive avarice, impatience, anxiety, or weakness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse itself serves as its definition and that it refers to the unbeliever or polytheist, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Jaza'iri take it as describing human nature in general. The exception made for those who pray is understood by the scholars as referring to those who keep up their prayer. Ibn Mas'ud takes this to mean observing the prescribed times, 'Uqba ibn 'Amir takes it to mean not turning one's face during prayer, and Ibn Jurayj takes it to mean frequent voluntary prayer. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that faith corrects this natural inclination, teaching the believer to endure trials patiently and to give thanks and share when blessed. Commentators agree that the trait is blameworthy, and they present prayer, the obligatory alms, patience and gratitude as the means of overcoming it, while differing on the meaning of some words and on how broadly the verse applies.

This verse makes an exception to the blameworthy traits described just before it, naming those who are spared the anxious and grasping nature of man. Commentators explain that hal', the trait described, is excessive distress when harm strikes and stinginess or grasping when good comes, a definition that Ibn Abbas gives through these two behaviours. Nearly all agree that the exception concerns those who pray, but they differ on who exactly is meant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean those who perform the obligatory prayers, while Ibn Mas'ud stresses keeping to the prescribed times, and Ibn Jurayj understands those who multiply voluntary prayers. Uqba ibn Amir links constancy in prayer to not turning the head right or left during it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that constancy means persisting without neglecting the prayer, and that guarding it means completing its conditions, pillars and recommended details. Some say the verse means believers in general, since their trust in God lets them overcome excessive distress. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that this trait is created by God just as the human being is, and that distress reveals weak faith in divine decree.

This verse describes the worshippers whom God exempts from the description of man as restless: prone to panic when harm touches him and tight-fisted when good comes his way. Nearly all commentators agree that constancy in prayer means performing it faithfully and on time without neglect. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Kathir stress keeping to the prescribed times and obligations, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as a steady devotion that is not distracted by other matters, and Ibn al-Jawzi links the root to the idea of stillness.

The scholars differ on how this constancy is to be understood. Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi take it to mean the five obligatory prayers, and al-Sam'ani reports the same view. Ibn Juzayy sees it as lasting perseverance throughout life. Ibn Jurayj, al-Hasan and al-Qurtubi emphasise performing many voluntary prayers. Uqba ibn Amir, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understands it as not turning the head right or left during prayer, a view also recorded by Ibn al-Qayyim.

The meaning of the word halu' itself varies in the commentaries: al-Mawardi lists stinginess, greed, impatience and weakness, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe it as intense anxiety combined with greed. Al-Zamakhshari argues that this disposition is innate and that the believers overcome it through discipline.

The commentators agree that those who keep up their prayer are distinguished by composure and generosity, and Ibn Kathir notes that prayer is mentioned both at the start and at the end of this list of qualities, which shows its high rank.

This verse describes those who are spared the human defect of hala', the excessive anxiety in hardship and stinginess in ease that the preceding verses portray. It says that those who set aside in their wealth a known right, a determined share, give it to the one who asks and to the one who is deprived. The commentators differ on what this right is. Qatada, Ibn Sirin, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi hold that it is the obligatory zakat, since it is fixed and known, and al-Qurtubi argues that a voluntary amount varying with need could not be called known. By contrast, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata', al-Nakha'i and Ibn Umar, and al-Sha'bi, say that there is a right beyond zakat, such as keeping ties of kinship, hosting a guest or helping a needy person. The solicitor is the one who asks, while the deprived is the one who holds back from asking out of modesty and is thought to be rich. On this second term the views are many: some take it to mean the poor man who has no share in the spoils, others the one whose property has been destroyed or whose livelihood has failed, and al-Sha'bi confessed he could not determine its meaning. The other qualities listed in the surrounding verses, faith in the Day of Judgement, fear of God's punishment, guarding chastity, keeping trusts and covenants, giving true testimony and maintaining the prayer, are broadly agreed upon by the exegetes.

This verse describes humans as naturally prone to anxiety at misfortune and to stinginess when blessed, and it exempts those who pray constantly. Among the exempted are those who set aside a known portion of their wealth for the beggar and the deprived. The commentators differ on what this portion is. Qatada, Ibn Sirin, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the obligatory zakat, because it is fixed and known, whereas Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Ibn 'Umar hold it to be a right beyond zakat, such as kinship ties, hospitality or helping the needy. Ibn 'Atiyya prefers this second view, arguing that the surah is Meccan while zakat was defined only in Medina. The beggar (sa'il) is generally agreed to be the one who asks. The deprived (mahrum) receives several explanations: for Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and others, he is the destitute man with no share in spoils or in community wealth; for Qatada, he is the modest person who refrains from asking and is taken for rich; for Ibn Zayd, he is one whose crops were destroyed; al-Sha'bi said he could not determine who he was. The following verses link these traits to faith in the Day of Judgement and fear of God's punishment, which no one may consider secure.

This part of the verse describes those who affirm the Day of Judgment, meaning they believe in resurrection, reckoning and recompense, and places them among the people of praiseworthy qualities that stand against the anxiety described just before. Commentators explain this belief as faith in resurrection, gathering and recompense; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi agree on this meaning. Ibn Kathir adds that such believers act like people who hope for reward and fear punishment. Al-Biqa'i holds that genuine belief shows itself in good deeds and preparation for the day of presentation, while one who professes it only with the tongue gains nothing from it. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take the same view, describing believers who exert themselves in acts of obedience out of hope for the reward of the hereafter. Al-Shinqiti simply states that the Day of Religion is the Day of Reckoning. The commentators do not differ on the sense of the phrase itself, but on how this belief becomes visible in conduct. Sayyid Qutb explains that faith in the Last Day changes the believer's view of the world: he does not panic at hardship nor cling excessively to wealth, because he sees worldly life as temporary. This quality thus connects with those that follow it, such as fear of God's punishment and guarding one's trusts and promises.

This verse describes the believers who are mushfiqun, meaning fearful and apprehensive of the punishment of their Lord. Al-Tabari explains that they dread the punishment of the Hereafter, and out of this fear they neglect no obligation and overstep no limit set by God. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and the Jalalayn share this plain meaning of fear, and Ibn Kathir adds that no one can feel safe from God's punishment unless God grants him security. The following phrase, that the punishment of their Lord is not to be taken for granted, is read by al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi as a warning that no one, however devout, should feel secure, and that a believer should keep a balance between fear and hope. Al-Razi explains that this fear arises from the possibility of falling short in duties or committing forbidden acts, so that a person can never be certain he has fully discharged what is owed to God. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi say they fear even though they do good works, belittling their deeds before God's majesty. Al-Biqa'i holds that the fear concerns both this world and the next, and that it is directed at a Lord who is also their benefactor. Sayyid Qutb sees this as a higher stage than mere belief in the Day of Judgment, reflecting a heightened sensitivity to falling short. Al-Sam'ani cites a report from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that on the Day of Resurrection the fearful will be gathered under the protection of the Merciful.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of those who pray, whom God excepts from the restless and anxious nature of man. Its meaning is that no one should feel safe from the punishment of his Lord, however much he obeys, so the believer should remain between fear and hope. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold this reading, and al-Razi adds that the fear comes from the awareness that one can never be sure of having fulfilled every duty fully. On the meaning of the word itself they do not disagree. They do differ on the verses just before it. For the "known right" in the wealth of the righteous, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi cite Qatada and Ibn Sirin who identify it with the obligatory zakat, while Mujahid, Ata' and al-Nakha'i, as well as reports from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, hold it to be a right beyond zakat. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy prefer the first view, since the text calls this right "known". Ibn 'Atiyya and others note that the surah is Meccan. As for the "deprived" (al-mahrum), some take him to be the poor man who refrains from asking, others the one who has no share of the booty, and others the one who has suffered a loss. No commentator decides between these readings.

This verse describes the believers who guard their private parts from everything God has forbidden. They use them only with their wives and their possessed slave-women, and they are not blamed for this. Whoever seeks beyond that is among the transgressors. The commentators broadly agree that guarding here means protecting oneself from fornication and what leads to it, and that the exception covers the wife and the slave-woman. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di conclude that the verse excludes temporary marriage (mut'a), since the woman taken in this way is neither a wife nor a slave-woman. Al-Sam'ani reports that A'isha and Ibn Umar rejected it on this basis. Ibn Sa'di adds that guarding also means not looking at or touching what is unlawful. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the same reading was given by Ibn Umar and others. Al-Razi focuses instead on the fear of God's punishment and on the place of the verse among the qualities of believers. Al-Alusi and Abu Hayyan understand the term as keeping sexual intercourse within what is permitted. Al-Hasan al-Basri took the phrase to refer to the private parts of clothing, but most read it as the act of intercourse. The verse is read in contrast with the unbelievers described earlier, who are greedy, anxious and stingy.

This verse describes believers who guard their private parts, except with their wives or with those whom their right hands possess, and who are not blameworthy for this. The commentators agree that wives and slave-women are the lawful outlets, and that mentioning them is an exception to the duty of chastity. Al-Tabari explains that the phrasing carries an implied negation: they are not blamed for not guarding themselves with these. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn and al-Nasafi, take what the right hand possesses to mean female slaves. Ibn Sa'di draws from the verse the prohibition of temporary marriage (mut'a), since such a partner is neither a wife nor an owned slave, and al-Sam'ani reports the same conclusion from Ibn 'Uyayna, 'A'isha and Ibn 'Umar. He also relates Ibn 'Uyayna's view that a man is not blamed for having up to four wives or any number of slave-women. Al-Biqa'i explains the choice of the word ma, normally used for non-rational beings, as a way of describing slave-women. Al-Razi reads verses twenty-nine to thirty-one together, concluding that whoever seeks beyond these limits is a transgressor. Al-Jaza'iri restricts slave-women to those acquired through jihad or lawful purchase, and Sayyid Qutb links slavery to the rules for prisoners of war.

This part of the verse says that whoever seeks sexual gratification beyond a wife or what the right hand possesses has exceeded the limit, and such people are the transgressors who turned what God made lawful into what He forbade. The commentators read the verse within a list of the believers' qualities, which opens with prayer and charity and closes with guarding the prayer. Al-Tabari explains that what lies beyond this means any union sought outside the wife or the slave woman, and that those who do so are the blameworthy. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree on this meaning, and al-Qurtubi adds that the phrase "they are not blamed" applies only within the permitted bounds. Al-Nasafi draws from it the prohibition of temporary marriage, intercourse with males or animals, and masturbation, while Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a warning against corrupting lineages and family order. Al-Jaza'iri counts this prohibition among the eight qualities that form a spiritual remedy. The commentators agree on the apparent sense, but differ on the details of its legal implications and scope.

This verse describes believers who guard the trusts entrusted to them, whether duties owed to God or goods and secrets given by people, and who keep their pledges to God and to others. They bear witness faithfully without concealing or altering it, and they observe the times and limits of their prayers. Their reward is to dwell in honoured gardens. The commentators broadly agree that the word amana covers both religious duties and the trusts of people, and that ahd covers promises made to God as well as to creatures. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Ibn Mas'ud took guarding prayer to mean observing its appointed times, while Uqba ibn Amir took it to mean not turning aside during prayer. On the testimony, Ibn Abbas understood it as the testimony of God's oneness, whereas most scholars took it as testimony before judges. Ibn Juzayy adds that it means being exact in giving testimony and not delaying it, and Ibn Atiyya cites hadiths on testimony and keeping promises without choosing between the readings. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di note that these qualities set believers apart from hypocrites. Some readings differ between singular and plural forms of these words, without changing the general meaning.

This verse describes one of the qualities of the believers whom God honours with the gardens of Paradise: they uphold their testimony firmly, neither concealing it nor altering it, and they give it as it is due whenever they are called to do so. Al-Tabari explains that they testify as required, without bias towards a relative or friend. Other commentators take it mainly as testimony before judges, which belongs to the trusts entrusted to people, and it is singled out to highlight its importance, since upholding it preserves rights. Ibn 'Abbas reads it more broadly as the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His messenger. Ibn Juzayy reports that the majority take it as testimony before judges, then distinguishes two meanings of upholding it: establishing it with certainty, or hastening to give it without hesitation when called. He adds that the duty to answer a summons varies according to the kind of right involved. The readings differ: Hafs, Ya'qub and Ibn 'Amir read the plural 'shahadatihim', while the others read the singular, which al-Razi and al-Wahidi consider preferable as a verbal noun. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that this verse belongs to a series of qualities, including prayer, almsgiving, belief in the Last Day, guarding chastity and faithfulness to trusts and covenants, which stand in contrast to the human nature described earlier as anxious and grasping.

This verse describes the believers who guard their prayer, meaning they perform it at its prescribed times and observe its limits, pillars and conditions as God has set them. It belongs to a series of qualities of the people of Paradise, and prayer both opens and closes that series. Al-Tabari explains that guarding it means not neglecting its appointed times and limits, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya include ablutions, bowing, prostration, recommended acts and proper conduct. Al-Alusi and al-Qasimi distinguish constancy (dawam), which concerns the prayers themselves, from guarding, which concerns their states and forms. Ibn Ashur notes that the present tense expresses a continual renewal of this vigilance and a refusal of negligence. The commentators agree that the verse is praise. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that mentioning prayer at the beginning and end of the qualities shows its importance. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that constancy may mean persistence in a deed, even a small one, as in the authentic hadith. Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Mas'ud understand the worshippers as those who perform the obligatory prayer on time. The commentators see this verse within a passage where God contrasts the qualities of believers with the conduct of the unbelievers who surrounded the Prophet, but read on its own the verse concerns only prayer and its preservation.

This verse announces the reward of those described in the preceding verses for their faithfulness and uprightness: they keep up their prayers, honour trusts and covenants, and bear witness truthfully. Al-Tabari explains that they dwell in gardens, and that God honours them with His own generosity. Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir add that they are honoured with various kinds of delights and pleasures. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that this description stands in contrast to the portrait of man, naturally prone to anxiety and miserliness, given just before. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi observe that the word "those" points to their high standing and rank, and that "in gardens" and "honoured" are two predicates. Ibn Ashur reads the verse as an explanatory transition that sets the believers' state against that of the disbelievers, who would wish to ransom themselves from punishment. Al-Biqa'i adds that they receive this reward already in this world, through the sweetness of closeness to God, and in the next through the welcome of the angels. The commentators agree that this is a promise to the believers, but differ on the qualities mentioned before. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand prayer as keeping its appointed times and limits. Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Shawkani, understands the testimony as testimony to God's oneness. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi hold that the known right in wealth is the obligatory zakat, while Mujahid and others extend it to other charity.

The commentators explain that God rebukes the disbelievers of Quraysh who gathered around the Prophet ﷺ hastening toward him with necks stretched and eyes fixed on him, in scattered circles to his right and left. They listened to the Quran in mockery and denial rather than seeking guidance. Al-Tabari and Qatada take «muhti'in» to mean hastening or intending, Ibn Zayd takes it to mean one who does not blink, al-Hasan to mean setting off, al-Kalbi to mean gazing at him in wonder, and 'Atiyya to mean turning away. As for «izin», most explain it as scattered groups, citing the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Jabir ibn Samura, «What is wrong with you that I see you in scattered circles?», as recorded by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. Al-Zamakhshari traces the word to 'izwa, since each group claims kinship with someone other than the others.

On the verse «Does every one of them hope to enter a garden of bliss?», Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and others report that the idolaters said that if these people entered Paradise as Muhammad claims, they would enter before them. The reply «No» rejects this. The commentators differ on «We created them from what they know»: al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it as a base drop of semen, al-Baghawi as the stages of conception, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy see it as belittling humankind and as evidence for resurrection. For Ibn Juzayy, entry to Paradise is earned through faith and righteous deeds. The majority reading is the passive «yudkhala», which al-Hasan and Talha read in the active voice, and al-Tabari prefers the majority reading.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Quraysh who gathered around the Prophet ﷺ while he recited the Qur'an. They rushed towards him with outstretched necks and clustered on his right and left in circles and small groups, listening in order to mock his words. God asks, with surprise, whether each of these disbelievers hopes to enter the Garden of bliss. He answers that all of them share the same origin and were created from a base drop, so no one earns Paradise by lineage but by faith and good deeds. The scholars differ on the meaning of 'izin. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean scattered groups in circles, while Ibn Abbas describes bands of people who turn away and ridicule him. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir link the word to the root meaning kinship or affiliation, each group claiming a different allegiance. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite a report from Abu Hurayra and Jabir ibn Samura in which the Prophet ﷺ asks his companions why he sees them in scattered circles. As for muhti'in, al-Akhfash and al-Tabari read it as hastening, ʿAṭiyya as turning away, al-Kalbi as gazing in wonder, and Qatada as heading towards him. Regarding 'what they know', most understand the base drop of semen, while some take it to mean commandments and reward and punishment. This range of views shows that the meanings are close overall.

This verse rebukes the disbelievers of Mecca for their hope of entering the Garden of bliss. They gathered around the Prophet ﷺ, to his right and left, in scattered circles, listening in order to mock him and saying that if the believers were to enter Paradise, they would enter before them. The reply is a firm 'no', followed by a reminder of their origin: they were created from a base drop, so no one earns Paradise through birth or rank, but through faith and righteous deeds. The commentators agree on the general sense of rejection and rebuke of arrogance, and on the argument for resurrection drawn from the first creation, since the One who created once can recreate. They differ on the phrase 'mimma ya'lamun'. Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as the impure seminal drop, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as a delicate allusion to the lowly origin of man, and others, including al-Qurtubi, take it to mean 'among those who know and reason, and not like beasts', or 'for the sake of what they do', referring to commands and reward. On recitation, al-Tabari adopts the majority reading 'yudkhala' in the passive, judging it the consensus, while Hasan and Talha read it in the active voice. As for 'izin', most explain it as scattered groups, and al-Zamakhshari links it to a root meaning to be attributed to another, each group being affiliated to a different leader. Al-Razi connects the verse both to the denial of resurrection and to the scorn the mockers showed toward the believers.

The commentators explain that the verse "No! Indeed We created them from that which they know" is a rebuke to the disbelievers who hoped to enter Paradise. The phrase "that which they know" means that they were created from a filthy drop they are well aware of, which gives them neither nobility nor a claim to Paradise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that entry into Paradise depends on obedience and faith, not merely on being created. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi read the clause as the reason for the rebuke, while Qatada takes it as a reminder to the son of Adam of his impure origin, so that he may fear God. Ibn Ashur and al-Razi draw from it an argument for the resurrection: whoever could create man from a drop can bring him back. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the vagueness of the phrase signals shame at that origin. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi report that "ma" may mean "for the sake of", that is, for worship and action, or "among those who know", meaning rational beings rather than animals. The commentators agree that the verse opposes pride based on lineage and that standing before God rests on faith and good deeds.

God swears by the Lord of the easts and the wests, meaning the risings and settings of the sun through the year or of the stars, that He is able to destroy these mockers and bring in better people in their place, more obedient to Him, and that nothing escapes Him or overcomes Him in what He wills. The commentators see this as a reply to the pagans who gathered in circles around the Prophet ﷺ, mocking the Qur'an and claiming they would enter Paradise before the believers; the answer reminds them that they were created from a base drop and that Paradise is earned through obedience, not claimed. Ibn Kathir takes the replacement to mean the resurrection with better bodies, while al-Razi notes that such a replacement did not occur, since the unbelievers died in disbelief, and that the threat was meant to call them to faith. Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, speaks of three hundred and sixty openings through which the sun rises, a report al-Tabari himself regards as garbled in its poetic form. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read the words «leave them to plunge and play» as a warning, and most scholars hold that their apparent tolerance was abrogated by the verse of the sword; al-Baghawi reports the same view, while Ibn al-Jawzi argues that abrogation is pointless if the threat concerns the Day of Judgment. All agree that the rising from the graves is in haste, as if rushing to their idols or a banner, with downcast eyes and humiliation covering them.

God swears by the Lord of the easts and the wests, meaning the rising and setting points of the sun across the year, that He is able to destroy these disbelievers and bring in people better than them, and that nothing escapes Him or prevents Him when He wills something. The commentators agree that the verse answers the mockers among the Quraysh who gathered around the Prophet ﷺ to ridicule his words and claimed they would enter Paradise before the believers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the sun rises each day from a different point in the year, and Ibn Kathir considers the more apparent meaning to be that God will restore people in bodies better than these, while al-Tabari prefers the sense of a people who will obey Him. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Zamakhshari take the verse as an argument for resurrection from the original creation out of a vile drop. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the threat in 'leave them to plunge and play' was abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur suggest the replacement may never have occurred, since most of the polytheists died in disbelief. To describe the Day of Judgment, the commentators say people will rush out of their graves as if hastening to a banner or an idol, and the word nusub is read in several ways; Mujahid and al-Kalbi understand it as a standard or a stone marker, while Abu 'Amr takes it to mean the hunter's net. Their eyes will be humbled and abasement will cover them.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to leave the disbelievers to their idle talk and their play in this world, until they meet the Day they have been promised, the Day of Judgment. Most commentators read the command as a threat rather than a general permission. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others explain that khawd means empty and confused talk, and la'b means frivolity and mockery. Al-Tabari and al-Shawkani say the addressees are the Quraysh of Mecca, who gathered in scattered circles around the Prophet to listen and ridicule his words. All agree that the promised day is the Day of Resurrection, and the verse describes them rushing out of their graves as if hurrying toward a idol or sign they used to worship, a detail that al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy connect to their former idols. On abrogation, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, while Ibn 'Ashur rejects this and reads it as an instruction to disregard their obstinacy. Al-Razi adds that the replacement threatened earlier did not occur, since these people died in disbelief.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when people rush out of their graves as if hurrying toward a marked goal. The commentators generally understand it as a hasty march toward the summons to the gathering place. On the word nusub, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain it as a sign, banner or target one heads for, following Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak, while al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Zamakhshari, who read it with both vowels, take it as an idol or a standing stone that the people used to worship and hurry to touch first. The verb yufdiduna means to hasten, a sense supported by verses of Arabic poetry quoted by al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan. As for their lowered gazes, commentators speak of humiliation, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi describe the disgrace that covers them, while Qatada says it is a darkening of the faces. The day in question is the Resurrection, which the polytheists of Mecca denied. Several scholars link the passage to the disbelievers who gathered in circles around the Prophet, mocking him, and see the verse as a warning that such mockers will not enter Paradise by their empty hopes.

This verse describes the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they emerge from their graves in haste, as if rushing toward a raised standard or an idol they used to worship. The commentators agree that their eyes will be lowered and humbled by what they see, that humiliation will cover them, and that this is the day they were promised in the world and used to deny. Abu al-'Aliya, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi explain the verb yufdiun as hastening, running and racing one another, while al-Hasan al-Basri describes people pressing forward to touch their idol, each wanting to be first. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the sense of a marker or goal to run toward, whereas Muqatil and al-Kisa'i take it to mean the idols they worshipped. On the reading of the word nusub, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that most readers vocalise it with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the sad, that Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read it with a damma on both letters, and Ibn Atiyya holds that these forms all mean the thing set up. Al-Mawardi explains khushu' as abasement and rahaq as covering, which Qatada takes to mean blackened faces. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir understand the lowered gaze as submission born of fear of punishment, while Ibn al-Qayyim sees both an outward humiliation and an inward one. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the past tense used for the promise expresses certainty that it will come to pass.
